As the Earth Warms, the Threat of Mosquito-Borne Diseases Expands 
 KESEHATAN MASYARAKAT As the Earth Warms, the Threat of Mosquito-Borne Diseases Expands
 The life cycle of mosquitoes is heavily influenced by temperature, rainfall patterns, and weather conditions. As a result, the threat of mosquito-borne diseases is increasing amid climate change.
 15 Nov 2026 10:32 WIB · Kesehatan 
 CENTERS FOR DISEASE CONTROL AND PREVENTI
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Deonisia Arlinta 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x Climate change affects all aspects of human life. In addition to its environmental impact, the climate crisis is also having a tangible effect on human health. The patterns of disease transmission, particularly vector-borne diseases spread by mosquitoes, are becoming increasingly difficult to predict.
 Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and increasingly unpredictable weather have impacted the life cycle of mosquitoes. The areas suitable for disease vector breeding are expanding, a situation exacerbated by high levels of global human mobility.
 This situation presents a challenge in efforts to control mosquito-borne diseases, such as dengue fever and malaria. New adaptations are inevitable.
 The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that over 17 percent of infectious diseases are transmitted through vectors such as mosquitoes, ticks, and flies. The incidence of dengue has also seen a significant rise globally in recent decades, with reported cases increasing from 505,430 in 2000 to 5.2 million in 2019.
 Dengue cases have spread to areas previously undocumented, including Europe, the Eastern Mediterranean, and South America. According to the BBC, the Aedes aegypti mosquito was first discovered breeding in London, England.
 A similar threat is occurring in Indonesia. Data from the Ministry of Health indicates that dengue fever cases have fluctuated over the past five years, with the highest number reported in 2024. That year, there were 257,271 recorded cases of dengue fever, resulting in 1,461 deaths.
 By 2025, the number of cases had decreased to 170,798, with 703 reported deaths. From 2026 until October, the total cases reached 98,946, resulting in 265 fatalities. The transmission of dengue fever has spread across 467 districts and cities in 33 provinces.
 Other mosquito-borne diseases also warrant attention. The number of malaria cases surged from 304,055 in 2021 to 706,297 in 2025, with approximately 95 percent of cases originating from Papua. Controlling malaria in high-endemic areas like Papua remains a significant challenge.
 The Director of Applied Climate Services at the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), Marjuki, stated in a phone interview from Jakarta on Thursday (12/11/2026) that changes in temperature and rainfall patterns in Indonesia must be taken into account to understand the transmission patterns of mosquito-borne diseases.
 Observations conducted over the past 45 years, from 1981 to 2025, indicate an average temperature increase of approximately 1.04 degrees Celsius in Indonesia.
 The year 2024 is set to be the hottest on record, with an average temperature reaching 27.5 degrees Celsius, an anomaly of 0.8 degrees Celsius compared to the previous period from 1991 to 2020. According to a report from the Ministry of Health, the highest transmission of dengue fever also occurred in that year.
 In addition to temperature, Marjuki noted that rainfall patterns in several regions of Indonesia have increased. This is particularly evident in Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku, and Papua, where rainfall patterns have shown an upward trend of up to 30 millimeters per year from 1981 to 2025.
 Mosquito life cycle
 Climatic factors such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall influence the life cycle and development of disease vectors, such as the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which transmits dengue fever, and the Anopheles mosquito, which transmits malaria. Increased temperature and humidity accelerate the mosquito's reproductive cycle and the incubation period for pathogens within the mosquito's body.
 "As a result, the transmission of the dengue virus and malaria parasites to humans can occur more rapidly. Additionally, rainfall plays a crucial role. The proliferation of open water pools and remnants of rainwater, particularly in endemic areas, creates an ideal habitat for the breeding of malaria vectors," said Marjuki.
 According to him, these conditions could trigger a spike in the population density of Anopheles mosquitoes and an increase in malaria cases. Furthermore, the transmission of mosquito-borne diseases is also influenced by climate.
 When El Niño occurs, drought conditions will prolong, prompting people to store more water in containers. However, Aedes aegypti mosquito eggs can survive dry conditions and stick to the walls of water containers.
 When it rains, the eggs will hatch, leading to an increase in the mosquito population in the area. As a result, spikes in dengue fever cases typically occur during the transition from the dry season to the rainy season. The surges in dengue cases in 2016, 2019, and 2024 coincided with El Niño periods.
 Meanwhile, the La Niña phenomenon, characterized by prolonged and heavy rainfall, also impacts mosquito habitats. The increase in stagnant water, which serves as breeding grounds for mosquitoes, is expected to rise during rainy conditions.
 Marjuki stated that temperature changes could make highland areas, which were previously too cold for mosquitoes to thrive, warmer and more suitable for them. Mountain regions that were not previously endemic to dengue transmission may now face an increased risk of the disease.
 "Climate projections show that by 2050, the spread of the Aedes aegypti mosquito (DHF) and malaria vectors is expected to expand to mid-latitude regions and higher elevations in the mountains from its original habitat," he said.
 "This threat is dangerous because communities in highland areas have historically never been exposed, so they do not have endemic immunity to fight off dengue fever or malaria," said Marjuki.
 Climate projections indicate that by 2050, the spread of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes (which transmit dengue fever) and malaria vectors is expected to expand into mid-latitude regions and higher elevations in mountainous areas.
 Triwibowo Ambar Garjito, a principal research expert at the Center for Public Health and Nutrition Research at the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), stated that climate change can affect the ability of mosquitoes to adapt and expand their habitat. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which play a role in transmitting dengue, are able to adapt to human-created environments.
 Temperature changes can favor mosquito habitats. Several reports indicate that the Aedes albopictus mosquito has been found in cool, subtropical climates where it had previously been unheard of.
 "These mosquitoes have become more adaptable to conditions that previously wouldn't have been suitable habitats. Now, Aedes mosquitoes can easily breed in these various habitats," he said.
 Uncertain
 Erni Juwita Nelwan, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Indonesia's Faculty of Medicine, explained that changes in weather and climate due to climate change significantly impact the transmission patterns of mosquito-borne diseases. Currently, there is no longer a transmission cycle for dengue fever during the rainy season.
 Unpredictable weather patterns have contributed to erratic disease transmission. Changes in rainfall and temperature have made it increasingly difficult to predict the boundaries between the rainy and dry seasons, potentially extending the period of disease transmission.
 "The most noticeable impact is the disruption of the five-year cycle of dengue fever. The rainfall pattern has changed. Now, cases fluctuate throughout the year, no longer limited to the end of the year and the beginning of the rainy season," he stated.
 Rising temperatures also impact the life cycle of mosquitoes and the ability of pathogens to reproduce within their vectors. At warmer temperatures, specifically between 25 and 29 degrees Celsius, the development of mosquitoes from eggs to adults can accelerate, shortening both the egg maturation cycle and the incubation period for the dengue virus and Plasmodium parasites.
 Erni stated that seasonal changes also affect the transmission of malaria. The impact of rainfall on malaria transmission is evident in several regions, including North Sumatra, Lampung, and the Bukit Menoreh area in Central Java. Environmental changes have created increasingly suitable habitats for malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
 However, climate change is not the sole factor determining the spread of mosquitoes and the diseases they carry. The transmission of diseases is also influenced by increasing human mobility, expanded trade and transportation, urbanization, as well as land use changes and deforestation. The interactions among humans, vectors including mosquitoes, and the environment are becoming increasingly close.
 The increasing mobilization of residents significantly impacts the transmission of diseases in areas that previously reported few cases. Individuals infected with malaria, including asymptomatic carriers, can transport the parasite to other regions. If the destination has suitable conditions and transmission vectors, a chain of transmission can develop.
 Furthermore, increased forest clearing and plantation activity can increase the risk of disease transmission, particularly malaria. Forests and plantations are generally habitats for the Anopheles mosquito. As more forest is cleared due to the expansion of plantation activity, the risk of transmission will increase.
 Control strategy
 According to Erni, climate change is making the control of vector-borne diseases increasingly challenging, with transmission patterns becoming harder to predict. However, disease control programs still tend to be implemented only after cases have risen. The changing weather and climate conditions demand more proactive and sustainable planning for disease management.
 "Vector-borne diseases are becoming increasingly threatening because they are increasingly difficult to control and increasingly unpredictable. Modifying disease control programs must be considered now. We can no longer conduct business as usual," he said.
 To address this, efforts to control dengue fever and malaria through enhanced surveillance systems need to be strengthened. The integration of climate-based early warning systems can also be implemented by combining climate anomaly predictions from BMKG with case surveillance data from community health centers and hospitals.
 In addition, mapping of high-risk areas using geographic information systems should be implemented down to the sub-district and village levels to ensure that interventions are tailored to the specific conditions of those areas.
 Routine monitoring must also be conducted without adhering to previous seasonal patterns, particularly in monitoring mosquito larvae density, periodically testing insecticide resistance status, and detecting shifts in dengue virus serotypes in regional laboratories.
 Erni emphasized that the government's commitment must be translated into policies and concrete actions that effectively control diseases. "The government's commitment should be translatable, starting from the attention given to policy and regulation development, to actions that truly have a significant impact on disease control," she stated.
